1.e4 e5 2.Nf3.strategy: The natural developing move: it attacks the e5 pawn, brings a knight into play and prepares castling. White keeps every plan open, from pressure on e5 to an attack on f7 or a central break with d4, and Black has to deal with the pawn first. The only cost is that the knight blocks the f-pawn, so f4 is out for now.

1.e4 e5 2.Bc4.strategy: Aims the bishop at f7 and stops ...d5 for the moment, while keeping the f-pawn free, so White can build up quietly or go for f4 later. The bishop can become a target for gains of time, and with no piece attacking e5 Black develops without pressure, so White gets a flexible game that is rarely forcing.

1.e4 e5 2.Nc3.strategy: Defends e4 with a piece and keeps the f-pawn free, so White can still treat it as a delayed King's Gambit with f4 or develop quietly. It blocks the c-pawn and puts no pressure on e5, so Black can equalise with accurate play: the move offers flexibility rather than an advantage.

1.e4 e5 2.f4.strategy: Offers a pawn to pull Black's e-pawn away from the centre and open the f-file, aiming for a pawn centre and an attack on f7. The cost is White's own king: the e1-h4 diagonal is open. The game tends to be sharp and double-edged, risky rather than recommended.

1.e4 e5 2.d4.strategy: Strikes at the centre at once and aims to open lines for quick development. But with no knight on f3 only the queen can recapture on d4, and Black attacks it with a gain of time. White can castle long and attack, yet Black develops easily, so the move is sound but not recommended.

1.e4 e5 2.d3.name: King's Pawn Game: Leonardis Variation
1.e4 e5 2.d3.strategy: Supports e4 and frees the c1-bishop for a solid set-up. But the pawn shuts the king's bishop's diagonal, and Black takes equal space in the centre. Sound but passive, so it is not recommended.

1.e4 e5 2.Bb5.name: Portuguese Opening
1.e4 e5 2.Bb5.strategy: Aims for a Ruy Lopez-type bishop on b5 while keeping the f-pawn free for f4. Without Nf3 there is no pressure on e5, so Black has a free hand and can even gain time against the bishop. Playable, though Black gets an easy game.

1.e4 e5 2.Qh5.strategy: Attacks e5 and f7 at once, hoping for a quick mate on f7 if Black is careless. Black defends the pawn with a developing move, and the early queen then becomes a target for attacks that gain time. It forces a few small concessions but gains no real advantage.

1.e4 e5 2.Ne2.name: Alapin's Opening
1.e4 e5 2.Ne2.background: Named after the Russo-Lithuanian player and openings analyst Semyon Alapin (1856–1923). It is rarely used, but occurred in Jacobsen–Ljubojević, Groningen 1970.
1.e4 e5 2.Ne2.strategy: A quiet knight move that keeps the f-pawn free for f4 or a slow set-up with g3, and avoids heavily analysed lines. But it blocks the king's bishop and the queen, and from e2 the knight controls nothing on Black's half of the board, so Black equalises easily. Playable as a surprise, not as a main weapon.

1.e4 e5 2.a3.name: King's Pawn Game: Mengarini's Opening
1.e4 e5 2.a3.background: Named after Ariel Mengarini, who advocated the move order 1.e4 e5 2.a3. The name is also given to the Vienna Game line 2.Nc3 Nf6 3.a3, where Hugh Myers inserted the knight moves before the a-pawn move.
1.e4 e5 2.a3.strategy: A waiting move that stops ...Bb4 and prepares b4, but develops nothing. Black takes the centre and in effect takes over the first move.

1.e4 e5 2.a4.strategy: Gains queenside space and prepares Ra3, but spends a tempo on the rim while the centre and development wait. Black develops at leisure.

1.e4 e5 2.b3.name: King's Pawn Opening
1.e4 e5 2.b3.strategy: Prepares Bb2 against e5, but that pawn is easily defended, and the bishop does little else. Meanwhile Black hits e4 at once, so White loses time without improving the centre.

1.e4 e5 2.c3.name: King's Pawn Game: MacLeod Attack
1.e4 e5 2.c3.strategy: Prepares d4 to build a broad centre, but takes c3 from the knight and delays development. Black strikes first, hitting e4 before White's centre is ready, and equalises without trouble.

1.e4 e5 2.c4.name: English Opening: The Whale
1.e4 e5 2.c4.strategy: Takes control of d5 but develops nothing and leaves holes on d4 and d3, since neither the c-pawn nor the e-pawn can guard them any more. Black can aim at d4, while the e4-pawn needs a defender.

1.e4 e5 2.f3.name: King's Pawn Game: King's Head Opening
1.e4 e5 2.f3.strategy: Supports e4, but takes f3 from the g1-knight and opens the e1-h4 diagonal, so ...Qh4+ becomes possible. Black develops freely or strikes in the centre and gets the easier game.

1.e4 e5 2.g3.strategy: Prepares Bg2, but with White's pawn on e4 the bishop's diagonal is blocked by its own pawn. Black hits e4 at once, and after 2...d5 3.exd5 Qxd5 the queen looks along the vacated long diagonal at the h1-rook.

1.e4 e5 2.h3.strategy: Takes g4 from Black's c8-bishop and king's knight, but develops nothing and does not fight for the centre. Black gets a free hand in the centre.

1.e4 e5 2.Na3.strategy: A rim knight that eyes c4 and b5 but little else. Black can trade it with ...Bxa3, and after bxa3 White is left with doubled, isolated a-pawns while Black develops freely in the centre.

1.e4 e5 2.Qe2.strategy: Defends e4, but blocks the f1-bishop and takes e2 from the g1-knight. Black develops freely, while the bishop stays shut in until the queen moves or White plays g3.

1.e4 e5 2.Qf3.name: Napoleon Opening
1.e4 e5 2.Qf3.background: The name came into use after publications of the mid-nineteenth century reported that Napoleon Bonaparte played it, in the game he lost to the chess automaton known as the Turk in Vienna in 1809.
1.e4 e5 2.Qf3.strategy: Eyes f7 and sets a trap, 2...Nc6 3.Bc4 Bc5?? 4.Qxf7#, which Black easily avoids by developing. The queen takes f3 from the g1-knight and can be harassed with tempo, so White falls behind in development.

1.e4 e5 2.Qg4.strategy: The queen attacks g7, which the f8-bishop defends, and walks into 2...d5, which uncovers the c8-bishop against the queen and attacks e4. After 3.exd5?? Bxg4 the queen is lost, so it must retreat at a cost in time.

1.e4 e5 2.Be2.strategy: Prepares castling but blocks the queen's diagonal to h5 and does nothing for the centre. Black takes the centre, and White is left with a passive set-up without an active bishop.

1.e4 e5 2.Bd3.name: King's Pawn Game: Tortoise Opening
1.e4 e5 2.Bd3.strategy: Defends e4 but blocks the d-pawn and with it the c1-bishop, so White's development stalls until the bishop moves again. Black develops in comfort and takes over the initiative.

1.e4 e5 2.Nh3.strategy: The knight heads for g5 or f4 but sits on the rim, and 2...d5 3.exd5 Bxh3 4.gxh3 Qxd5 wrecks White's kingside pawns and attacks the h1-rook. Black gets a free centre and easy development.

1.e4 e5 2.h4.strategy: Gains space on the rim and prepares h5 or a rook lift via h3, but does nothing for the centre or development. Black attacks e4 at once and gets a comfortable game, while the kingside, where White's king usually castles, is loosened.

1.e4 e5 2.b4.strategy: Offers the b-pawn with no development behind it: 2...Bxb4 wins it, and after 3.c3 the bishop retreats safely, leaving White without enough compensation.

1.e4 e5 2.g4.strategy: Gains kingside space but weakens f3, h3 and the long diagonal. After 2...d5 3.exd5 Qxd5 the queen attacks the h1-rook and Black takes the lead in the centre; the king's flank stays loosened for good.

1.e4 e5 2.Ke2.name: Bongcloud Attack
1.e4 e5 2.Ke2.background: The name is thought to come either from the Chess.com user “Lenny_Bongcloud”, who played it with little success, or from the word “bong”, implying that one would have to be intoxicated to take it seriously. Magnus Carlsen opened with it against Hikaru Nakamura at the Magnus Carlsen Invitational on 15 March 2021; Nakamura answered 2...Ke7 and the game was drawn by threefold repetition.
1.e4 e5 2.Ke2.strategy: Gives up castling and blocks both the queen and the king's bishop, so the king has to move again before White can develop normally. Black needs nothing special: quick development and an open centre are enough against the stranded king.

1.e4 e5 2.Ba6.strategy: Hangs the bishop: 2...bxa6 or 2...Nxa6 wins it for nothing, and White has no compensation for the lost piece.

1.e4 e5.name: Open Game
1.e4 e5.background: The Open Games, which begin 1.e4 e5, include many of the oldest and most deeply analysed openings in chess. 1...e5 was the usual answer to 1.e4 for centuries, until the Sicilian Defence became slightly more popular among tournament players in the mid-twentieth century.

1.e4 e5 2.Bb5 Bc5.strategy: A natural developing move: the bishop eyes f2 and the centre while White's bishop on b5 has little to aim at, since no black knight stands on c6 to be pinned. Black simply develops and is already the more comfortable side.

1.e4 e5 2.Bb5 Nf6.strategy: Develops and attacks the e4 pawn at once, which White now has to defend. The b5-bishop has no black knight to pin and does little; Black develops normally and can make use of the bishop's early excursion later.

1.e4 e5 2.Bb5 c6.strategy: The principled reply: it attacks the bishop at once, and with no knight on c6 the bishop has nothing to pin, so White loses time retreating. Black then builds a classical pawn centre and has a comfortable, simple game.

1.e4 e5 2.Bb5 Bc5 3.b4.name: Portuguese Opening: Miguel Gambit
1.e4 e5 2.Bb5 Bc5 3.b4.strategy: Offers the b-pawn to deflect Black's bishop, hoping for a tempo-gaining reply and a big centre. But the bishop on b5 does not help the attack as it would on c4, and Black simply takes the pawn: a dubious gambit.

1.e4 e5 2.Bb5 Bc5 3.Nf3.strategy: Develops and attacks the e5-pawn, which Black's last move left undefended, so Black must answer at once. With the knight out White can castle quickly and keeps the bishop on b5 ready to challenge a defender on c6. It gives the early bishop move a sensible point.

1.e4 e5 2.Bb5 Bc5 3.Nc3.strategy: Develops, guards the e4-pawn and defends the bishop on b5, so ...c6 no longer wins time outright, though it still drives the bishop away. A flexible, solid set-up, but it leaves e5 alone and Black's bishop keeps its sights on f2, so Black develops freely.

1.e4 e5 2.Bb5 Bc5 3.c3.strategy: Prepares d4 to hit the bishop on c5 and to build a broad pawn centre. The price is time and the c3 square, which the queen's knight would like to use, while the bishop on b5 stays exposed to ...c6 and Black's bishop already eyes f2: playable, but slower than simple development.

1.e4 e5 2.Bb5 Nf6 3.d4.name: Portuguese Opening: Portuguese Gambit
1.e4 e5 2.Bb5 Nf6 3.d4.strategy: Opens the centre at once, offering a pawn for activity instead of developing. Black's knight already attacks e4, and the b5-bishop has no knight to pin, so White's activity is limited: a risky try rather than a good one.

1.e4 e5 2.Bb5 Nf6 3.Nc3.strategy: Develops a piece and defends the pawn Black's knight attacks, the most natural reply. It also defends the bishop on b5, so ...c6 only asks it to move. White gets a solid, flexible set-up with the f-pawn still free for a later kingside break, and a quiet game in which the early bishop move has cost little.

1.e4 e5 2.Bb5 Nf6 3.Nf3.strategy: Develops and attacks e5, accepting that Black can take on e4 and that White then takes on e5 in return. The result is an open game with the pawns level, in which both sides have to watch the e-file and the centre.

1.e4 e5 2.Bb5 Nf6 3.d3.strategy: Defends e4 with a pawn and opens the c1-bishop's diagonal, a solid way to hold the centre without committing a knight. It is slow, though: Black can strike in the centre or develop freely, and the bishop on b5 still has no target.

1.e4 e5 2.c3 d5.strategy: The vigorous answer to a slow move: Black strikes at the centre before White has a piece out. After 3.exd5 Qxd5 the queen cannot be chased with Nc3, because the c3-pawn occupies that square, so Black recaptures with an active queen and a comfortable game.

1.e4 e5 2.c3 f5.name: King's Pawn Game: MacLeod Attack, Lasa Gambit
1.e4 e5 2.c3 f5.strategy: Hits e4 at once with the f-pawn, but it opens the e8-h5 diagonal in front of an undeveloped king, and 3.exf5 simply wins a pawn. Black has no lead in development to make up for it, so the gambit is more reckless than ambitious.

1.e4 e5 2.c3 Nf6.strategy: A sound alternative to the central thrust: Black develops with an attack on e4, so White has to defend the pawn or push on at once, and the slow c3 is not yet a useful move. The game stays flexible, with more pieces on the board than after ...d5.

1.e4 e5 2.c3 Nc6.strategy: Defends e5 with a developing move and lets White decide. The natural continuation reaches a known set-up in which White keeps the plan of building a broad pawn centre that the c3 move was made for. Black is not worse, but passes up the chance to punish the slow second move.

1.e4 e5 2.c3 d5 3.Qh5.strategy: Brings the queen out early to hit e5 and f7, but Black has developing replies that defend e5 or attack the queen. White has no other piece out to support the raid, so the queen loses time and Black takes the lead in development.

1.e4 e5 2.c3 d5 3.exd5.strategy: The simplest answer: White takes the pawn and Black usually recaptures with the queen. Without the knight tempo on c3 the queen is comfortable on d5 and Black develops freely, so White ends at best level, but the position is sound and free of risk.

1.e4 e5 2.c3 d5 3.Nf3.strategy: Develops and attacks e5, but ...dxe4 followed by Nxe5 and ...Qe7 attacks the knight again with a gain of time. After it moves, a d4 push is met by a capture en passant with a discovered check, so Black gets the better game.

1.e4 e5 2.c3 d5 3.Qh5 Bd6.name: King's Pawn Game: MacLeod Attack, Norwalde Gambit
1.e4 e5 2.c3 d5 3.Qh5 Bd6.strategy: Guards e5 with a developing move, so the queen's raid achieves nothing: Qxe5+ would lose the queen to Bxe5. The d5-pawn is left to be taken, but a knight is ready to hit the queen with tempo, so Black plays a gambit for a lead in development.

1.e4 e5 2.c3 d5 3.Qh5 Nc6.strategy: Defends e5 with a piece and develops, so the queen's raid has no target: Qxe5+ would just lose the queen. Black keeps the tension in the centre and gets ahead in development, while White has spent tempi on a queen sortie with nothing to show for it.

1.e4 e5 2.c3 d5 3.Qh5 dxe4.strategy: Takes the pawn at once, but 4.Qxe5+ takes one back with check, and Black must trade queens to keep the pawn on e4. Then Black has an advanced pawn to look after and no lead in development, while the developing replies keep far more.

1.e4 e5 2.c4 d5.name: King's Pawn Game: Bavarian Gambit
1.e4 e5 2.c4 d5.strategy: Attacks e4 at once, but the c4-pawn guards d5: 3.exd5 wins a pawn that Black cannot retake, since Qxd5 loses the queen to cxd5, and 3.cxd5 Qxd5 4.Nc3 chases the queen with a gain of time. Black pays for the centre thrust.

1.e4 e5 2.c4 Nf6.strategy: Develops and attacks the undefended e4 pawn at once, so White has to answer the threat before anything else. The c-pawn has already taken the f1-bishop's best diagonal, and Black gets an easy, active game.

1.e4 e5 2.c4 Nc6.strategy: Develops, defends e5 and eyes the hole on d4 that the c4 pawn leaves behind, a square White's pawns can no longer guard. There is no immediate threat, but Black has a comfortable game and the choice of how to meet White's set-up.

1.e4 e5 2.c4 Bc5.strategy: Develops the bishop on its most active diagonal, aimed at f2 and controlling d4, the square White's pawn structure can no longer guard. Black has a flexible, comfortable game with a free choice of how to complete development.

1.e4 e5 2.d3 Nf6.strategy: Develops a piece and pressures e4, which the d3-pawn has to keep defending. White's slow second move leaves Black free to claim the centre with the d-pawn next, so Black reaches easy equality with a sound, flexible set-up and no weaknesses.

1.e4 e5 2.d3 d5.strategy: Claims the centre at once, before White has developed anything. White can trade pawns, and Black recaptures with an active game and an easy equality; the price is that a queen recapture in the middle can be hit by a developing move.

1.e4 e5 2.d3 f5.name: King's Pawn Game: Clam Variation, King's Gambit Reversed
1.e4 e5 2.d3 f5.strategy: Hits e4 with the f-pawn, but d3 already guards that pawn, so the attack achieves nothing. White simply takes with 3.exf5, wins a pawn, and Black has opened the e8-h5 diagonal in front of an undeveloped king.

1.e4 e5 2.d3 d5 3.exd5.strategy: Settles the tension at once: Black has no piece that can retake yet, so the natural recapture is with the queen, which Nc3 then chases with tempo. The material is level, but White gains time and the solid d3 structure keeps the position safe.

1.e4 e5 2.d3 d5 3.Nf3.strategy: Develops with an attack on e5 and keeps the tension in the centre. The cost is that Black can exchange on e4 and, if White recaptures, trade queens, after which White must retake with the king and loses the right to castle, so Black gets an easy game.

1.e4 e5 2.d3 d5 3.Nd2.strategy: Guards e4 a second time with a piece and prepares to keep the pawn chain d3 and e4 intact. It blocks the queen's bishop and is passive, so Black has no problem taking the centre and equalising.

1.e4 e5 2.d3 d5 3.exd5 c6.strategy: Declines to recapture the d5-pawn and offers a second pawn instead, hoping for quick development. After dxc6 Nxc6 Black is a pawn down for a single developed piece, which White's solid set-up can absorb without difficulty.

1.e4 e5 2.d3 d5 3.exd5 Qxd5.strategy: Retakes at once with the queen and levels the material. It costs a tempo, since Nc3 attacks the queen, but the queen has safe retreats and Black keeps the pawn on e5 as a solid centre. The most direct way to equalise.

1.e4 e5 2.d3 d5 3.exd5 Nf6.strategy: Develops a piece and attacks the pawn on d5, aiming to win it back with a developing move. White can hold it with c4, though, and then Black has only a lead in development for the pawn, with no clear way to regain it.

1.e4 e5 2.d3 d5 3.exd5 c6 4.dxc6.strategy: Accepts the second pawn: after the recapture White keeps a clean extra pawn. The task is to finish development safely and keep the position closed enough that Black's lead in activity cannot turn into an attack.

1.e4 e5 2.d3 d5 3.exd5 c6 4.Nf3.strategy: Develops and eyes e5 instead of taking the second pawn. Black cannot retake on d5 without dropping e5, but can develop with the d5-pawn still under attack, so White must defend it or take on c6 later. Playable, but accepting the pawn at once is simpler.

1.e4 e5 2.d3 d5 3.exd5 c6 4.Nc3.strategy: Develops and adds pressure on d5 but leaves the gambit pawn alone. Black retakes with the c-pawn, the material is level again, and White is left with a normal, equal game.

1.e4 e5 2.d3 d5 3.exd5 c6 4.dxc6 Nxc6.name: King's Pawn Game: Weber Gambit
1.e4 e5 2.d3 d5 3.exd5 c6 4.dxc6 Nxc6.strategy: The natural recapture: it develops a piece, covers e5 and d4 and cuts the deficit to a single pawn. Black plays for quick development and open lines as compensation, and this is the most direct way to get them.

1.e4 e5 2.d3 d5 3.exd5 c6 4.dxc6 bxc6.strategy: Recaptures with the b-pawn to open the b-file and control d5 and b5, but Black is still a pawn down with a loose queenside and an isolated a-pawn. The pawn on c6 buys too little for that, and White is simply better.

1.e4 e5 2.d3 d5 3.exd5 c6 4.dxc6 Nf6.strategy: Ignores the pawn on c6 to develop. After cxb7 Bxb7 Black has the bishop on the long diagonal but is two pawns down, which is too much to pay for the lead in development against White's solid set-up.

1.e4 e5 2.d3 Nf6 3.f4.strategy: Attacks the e5-pawn, which no black piece defends yet, and aims for an open f-file. It loosens the king's side before any piece is out, and e4 is held only by the d-pawn, so Black can answer with active play and equalise comfortably.

1.e4 e5 2.d3 Nf6 3.Nf3.strategy: The natural developing move: it attacks the e5-pawn and makes Black spend a move defending it, while d3 keeps e4 safe. White builds a compact pawn chain on d3 and e4 and plays a slow, safe game in which Black equalises easily.

1.e4 e5 2.d3 Nf6 3.Be2.strategy: Develops the king's bishop behind the pawn chain and prepares to castle, keeping everything solid. It attacks nothing, so Black can take the centre with ...d5 at once, and White has to be content with equality.

1.e4 e5 2.d3 Nf6 3.Nc3.strategy: Develops a piece and adds control of e4 and d5, but blocks the c-pawn and allows ...Bb4, which pins the knight against the king. Sound, though less natural than developing the king's side first.

1.e4 e5 2.d3 Nf6 3.f4 Bc5.name: King's Pawn Game: Clam Variation, Radisch Gambit
1.e4 e5 2.d3 Nf6 3.f4 Bc5.strategy: Leaves e5 en prise on purpose and eyes the knight on g1 along the diagonal that f4 opened. But after 4.fxe5 the trick ...Nxe4 fails to 5.Qg4, which attacks g7 and d7, and Black is simply a pawn down with nothing to show for it.

1.e4 e5 2.d3 Nf6 3.f4 d5.strategy: Strikes in the centre at once: the e4-pawn is held by the d-pawn alone, and Black's pawn on d5 challenges it with the knight on f6 adding pressure. Black answers the flank pawn push with a central break before the loosened king's side can be exploited.

1.e4 e5 2.d3 Nf6 3.f4 exf4.strategy: Takes the pawn and opens the f-file, but the gain is temporary: White recaptures with the bishop, which develops at once. Black has a comfortable game with a free hand in the centre. Principled, though less ambitious than a central strike.

1.e4 e5 2.f3 Nf6.strategy: Develops and puts the e4 pawn under attack, a pawn only the f3 pawn holds. Natural and sound, but it does little with the weakened king's side, and White can reach a solid set-up without falling behind.

1.e4 e5 2.f3 d5.strategy: Strikes at e4 at once, but the centre opens before Black has developed: after 3.exd5 Black must regain the pawn, and White gets time to sort out the cramped set-up. Sound, but it lets White off lightly.

1.e4 e5 2.f3 Nc6.strategy: Develops and guards e5, preparing ...d5 to challenge the e4 pawn, which only the f3 pawn holds. Black plays the natural, solid way and keeps every option open; the cost is a tempo that lets White sort out the set-up.

1.e4 e5 2.f3 Bc5.strategy: Develops with several jobs: with f2 empty, the bishop reaches g1 and keeps White from castling short, and it controls d4 against the central break. It takes the best advantage of the weakened king's side and gives Black an easy game.

1.e4 e5 2.f3 Nf6 3.Bc4.strategy: Aims the bishop at f7, but it leaves e4 resting on the f3 pawn alone and invites ...d5, which hits the bishop and the e4 pawn together. With the king's diagonal weakened and the knight cramped, White drifts into a worse game.

1.e4 e5 2.f3 Nf6 3.Nc3.name: King's Pawn Game: King's Head Opening
1.e4 e5 2.f3 Nf6 3.Nc3.strategy: Develops and guards e4, so ...Nxe4 simply loses a piece. Sound, but it only defends: the f3 pawn still takes the best square from the king's knight, the king's diagonal stays open, and Black develops with the initiative.

1.e4 e5 2.f3 Nf6 3.d3.strategy: Supports e4 with a pawn and opens the c1-bishop, but it is passive: the f3 pawn still blocks the king's knight and weakens the king's diagonal, and Black develops freely with the initiative while White has spent a move on defence.

1.e4 e5 2.f3 Nf6 3.d4.strategy: Strikes at the centre at once, challenging e5 before Black's pieces settle. After ...exd4 the queen recaptures and can swing to f2, out of reach of ...Nc6, so the f3 pawn costs White little here. It is the one move that keeps the game level.

1.e4 e5 2.Qe2 Nc6.strategy: A natural reply: the knight defends e5 and takes a good square, while the queen on e2 stands in front of White's own bishop. Black develops comfortably and White has to decide what to do with the queen's placement.

1.e4 e5 2.Qe2 Nf6.strategy: Develops with a threat on e4, which only the queen defends, so the queen is tied to the pawn while Black keeps building. The knight takes its best square and White's early queen move starts to look like a loss of time.

1.e4 e5 2.Qe2 Bc5.strategy: Develops the bishop to an active diagonal aimed at f2 and keeps the knight's best square, f6, free. The queen on e2 blocks White's own king's bishop, so Black can develop at leisure and answer White's set-up as it appears.

1.e4 e5 2.Qe2 Nc6 3.c3.strategy: Prepares a broad pawn centre, but it spends a move on a pawn while the knight on b1 loses its natural square. A solid idea that needs the queen to stay out of trouble on the e-file.

1.e4 e5 2.Qe2 Nc6 3.Nf3.strategy: Develops and attacks e5, with the queen still guarding e4: the plain, natural way to treat the early queen move. White keeps the centre options open while Black has to keep e5 guarded.

1.e4 e5 2.Qe2 Nc6 3.Nc3.strategy: Develops and adds a second guard to e4, so the queen is no longer tied to the pawn. It blocks the c-pawn and gives up the broad pawn centre, leaving a flexible set-up in which White builds with pieces first.

1.e4 e5 2.Qe2 Nc6 3.c3 Nf6.strategy: Attacks the e4 pawn, which only the queen defends, and develops with tempo. Black pressures White's centre before the d-pawn can take control of it.

1.e4 e5 2.Qe2 Nc6 3.c3 d6.strategy: Supports e5 with a pawn, so the knight on c6 is free to move and the centre is firm. It shuts in the king's bishop for the moment: a solid, passive set-up that leaves White the choice of how to proceed.

1.e4 e5 2.Qe2 Nc6 3.c3 Bc5.strategy: Develops the bishop toward f2, but it can be hit at once by b4, which gains space with tempo. Black keeps the pieces active, but may have to spend time moving the bishop again.

1.e4 e5 2.Qe2 Nc6 3.c3 Nf6 4.Nf3.strategy: Develops and attacks e5, which Black has to keep guarded. With the c3 pawn already in place, White prepares a broad pawn centre, and Black must decide how to meet it.

1.e4 e5 2.Qe2 Nc6 3.c3 Nf6 4.d3.strategy: Supports e4 with a pawn, which frees the queen from guarding it, and opens the diagonal for the c1 bishop. A solid, patient set-up that takes the target away from the knight on f6 and keeps the centre intact, at the cost of a slower build-up.

1.e4 e5 2.Qe2 Nc6 3.c3 Nf6 4.d4.strategy: Strikes in the centre at once, but e4 is guarded only by the queen: after ...exd4 the knight on f6 and then ...Qe7 attack it twice, and Black wins a pawn. White's open centre and queen on the e-file do not make up for it.

1.e4 e5 2.Qe2 Nc6 3.c3 Nf6 4.Nf3 Bc5.strategy: Develops the bishop to an active diagonal aimed at f2 and prepares castling. Black keeps the pieces coming out and lets White decide whether to challenge the centre with a pawn.

1.e4 e5 2.Qe2 Nc6 3.c3 Nf6 4.Nf3 d6.strategy: Gives e5 a second guard with a pawn, so the centre is firm and the knight on c6 is free to move. It shuts in the king's bishop for now: solid and patient, with Black waiting for White to commit.

1.e4 e5 2.Qe2 Nc6 3.c3 Nf6 4.Nf3 Be7.strategy: Develops the bishop on a safe square and prepares castling, out of reach of a d4 or b4 pawn thrust. It gives up the active diagonal toward f2, so Black chooses safety over pressure.

1.e4 e5 2.Qe2 Nc6 3.c3 Nf6 4.Nf3 d5.strategy: Strikes at the centre at once, but it opens the e-file against Black's own king: after exd5 the queen on e2 pins the e5 pawn, so ...Nxd5? is met by d4, which wins it. Black has to recapture with the queen and stay under pressure.

1.e4 e5 2.Qe2 Nc6 3.c3 Nf6 4.Nf3 Bc5 5.d.strategy: Hits the bishop and opens the centre, but it is a pawn sacrifice that does not pay: after ...exd4 Black is a pawn up, and White's lead in development and the open e-file are thin compensation. Quiet development keeps the balance.

Supports e4 with a pawn, so the queen no longer has to guard it, and opens the c1-bishop. A solid, patient set-up: White declines the early tactics around e5 and f2, keeps the centre intact and develops at leisure, while Black has no difficulty equalising.

1.e4 e5 2.Qe2 Nc6 3.c3 Nf6 4.Nf3 Bc5 5.N.strategy: Grabs the e5 pawn, but the knight is exposed: after ...Nxe5 d4 forks bishop and knight, Black hits back with ...d5, and after dxe5 Nxe4 the king on e1 is under fire on f2. A sharp, level fight that needs exact calculation.

1.e4 e5 2.Qe2 Nc6 3.c3 Nf6 4.Nf3 Bc5 5.d.strategy: Accepts the offer and removes the pawn that attacked the bishop. Black is a pawn up for the moment, and has to meet White's regaining of it with a firm hand while the king is still in the middle.

Keeps the bishop and gives e5 a second guard, but the bishop blocks the d-pawn and leaves Black cramped. White pushes d5 to drive the knight back and takes space, while Black has passed up the free pawn on d4.

Moves the attacked bishop out of the pawn's reach and keeps it aimed at f2, but leaves e5 to the d-pawn: dxe5 wins a pawn, since ...Nxe5 loses a knight for it to Nxe5. Black's only compensation is activity against f2 with ...Ng4.
Retakes and attacks the bishop, but the pawn on d4 is weak: attacked by the bishop and the knight and defended once, it falls to ...Nxd4, and after the exchange Black is a clean pawn up.

Attacks the knight with a pawn the queen backs up on the e-file, a trap for the natural retreats ...Ng4 and ...Nd5. But Black has ...O-O, and if exf6 then ...Re8 pins the queen to the king, so Black keeps the extra pawn. A sharp try, not a way to equalise at once.
Regains the pawn with the knight, but the exchange on d4 only helps Black: ...Nxd4 cxd4 Bxd4 leaves Black an extra pawn and a well-placed bishop.

Hits the bishop with a flank pawn and keeps pressure on d4: Black must find ...Bb6, since taking on b4 gives up the bishop for two pawns. White then chases the knight with b5 and regains the pawn. Black's pieces stay more active, but this is the least costly way to pay for the gambit.

1.e4 e5 2.Qe2 Nc6 3.c3 Nf6 4.Nf3 Bc5 5.d.name: King's Pawn Opening: Van Hooydoon Gambit
1.e4 e5 2.Qe2 Nc6 3.c3 Nf6 4.Nf3 Bc5 5.d.strategy: Wins the pawn with an attack on the queen: the knight on d4 hits both e2 and f3. Black ends a clear pawn up, and White's only hope of compensation lies in the open centre and Black's king still in the middle.
Checks and develops with tempo, but it throws away Black's advantage: White blocks, the d4 pawn is no longer a target, and the position is level. Taking on d4 keeps the extra pawn.
Leaves the bishop on c5 attacked by the d4 pawn: dxc5 wins a piece for White, and Black gets little more than a pawn back.

1.e4 e5 2.Qg4 Nf6.strategy: Attacks the queen and develops a piece in the same move, so Black gains a tempo. The queen has to move again, so White spends two moves on it while nothing else is developed.

1.e4 e5 2.Qg4 d5.strategy: Opens the c8-bishop onto the queen and strikes at e4 in the same move, so the queen has to move again and Black takes the centre with tempo. It is the one real alternative to the knight attack, and the queen's early trip soon looks like lost time.

1.e4 e5 2.Qg4 Nc6.strategy: Defends e5 with a developing move and leaves the queen alone. Nothing hangs, since the bishop guards g7, but Black forgoes the tempo that attacking the queen would win, and White can use the time to bring out another piece.

1.e4 e5 2.Qg4 Nf6 3.Qf5.name: King's Pawn Opening: Speers
1.e4 e5 2.Qg4 Nf6 3.Qf5.strategy: Defends e4 and eyes the undefended e5 pawn, but ...Nc6 defends it with a developing move, and ...d5 then opens the c8-bishop against the queen. Having moved the queen twice, White is soon well behind in development.

1.e4 e5 2.Qg4 Nf6 3.Qg3.strategy: Keeps the queen on the board with a threat of its own: from g3 it eyes the pawns on e5 and g7. If Black takes on e4 with the knight, White takes e5 with check and the position levels out, though Black is ahead in development.

1.e4 e5 2.Qg4 Nf6 3.Qf3.strategy: Retreats to a square that defends e4, so no pawn is lost. The queen blocks the natural square of the g1-knight, though, and Black can keep gaining time with central pawn moves while White's remaining pieces are still at home.

1.e4 e5 2.Qg4 Nf6 3.Qe2.strategy: The calm retreat: the queen defends e4 and leaves the g1-knight its natural square. It has cost two moves, so Black is ahead in development and has the easier game, but White has no weakness and can catch up with sound play.
